newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - SAirGroup prepares for European turbulence.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - SAirGroup prepares for European turbulence.

text.p: SAirGroup, which includes flagcarrier Swissair, on Friday predicted turbulent European skies and said provisions of 300 million Swiss francs in 1996 should help it survive the coming industry shakeout.

The precautionary provisions, which pushed SAirGroup into a net loss of 497 million Swiss francs in 1996, are not earmarked for any specific cost-cutting measures, but can be used for any possible future plans, including cost-cutting at troubled Belgian partner Sabena SA.
"We are on target, but the race is getting tougher," chief executive Philippe Bruggisser told a news conference.

Last year was a difficult transition year for SAirGroup, which not only changed its corporate structure, but also cut the workforce at its core Swissair airline by 2,000 people in an attempt to stop the flow of red ink.

Despite a 40 percent improvement in group operating profit to 344 million francs, SAirGroup slid into a loss in 1996 and omitted a dividend payment due to the precautionary provisions of 300 million and a 267 million charge for writing down the value of its 49.5 percent stake in Sabena.
"It is possible -- we can't exclude it -- that further measures at Sabena will be necessary," Bruggisser said.

SAirGroup owns 49.5 percent of Sabena and fully wrote down the value of its stake in Sabena in 1996 -- 267 million francs -- reflecting Sabena's 1996 loss of 8.9 billion Belgian francs and an expected loss in 1997.
Bruggisser declined to make a profit forecast for SAirGroup for the current year, but said so far it was on target and he hoped to make progress this year in cutting Swissair's loss.

"We hope to be able to significantly improve the airline's result," Bruggisser said, noting Swissair's core flight operations lost some 120 million francs in 1996 and he was committed to his target of making it profitable by 1998.
"Maybe we have to take further hard measures to remain competitive. But I don't know when," Bruggisser said.
The skills required to improve Swissair's performance in a liberalised market will come from Jeffrey Katz, an executive from American Airlines, now chief operating officer of Swissair.

Katz, who only just arrived in Switzerland this month after 20 years in the U.S. airline industry, said air fares will become extremely important in Europe and it is "absolutely necesary to have sustainable and consistent profitability."
"But I think Swissair will be a survivor,," Katz added.

In addition to improving the competitiveness of Swissair, Bruggisser wants to strengthen cooperation with partner airlines and continue to expand the group's profitable and growing catering and duty-free activities.
In Europe Swissair has a partnership with Sabena and Austrian Airlines and worldwide it cooperates with Delta Air Lines and Singapore Airlines.
Finalisation of an open sky between the United States and Singapore should have a positive impact on the partnership between Singapore Airlines and Swissair.
"It opens up the possibility that Singapore Airlines will join the Atlantic Excellence," Bruggisser said.
The Atlantic Excellence group, which recently strengthened cooperation, comprises Swissair, Delta, Sabena and AUA.
SAirGroup now consists of four business segments with Swissair and Crossair airlines grouped in SAirLines and catering and duty-free activities in SAirRelations.
Although SAirLines accounts for 44 percent of the group's turnover, it only accounts for 22 percent of operating profits.
SAirRelations, which includes the world's second largest caterer Gate Gourmet and duty-free activities of Nuance, makes up 27 percent of group sales, but 48 percent of profits.
"When something is successful and profitable you want to expand that," Bruggisser said, adding that there were expansion possibilities in South America, Asia and Europe.
